**On Sourdough Starters**

Somewhere in a San Francisco bakery, there is a jar of flour and water that has been alive, in some sense, for more than a hundred and fifty years. No single yeast cell from its beginning survives, of course. The organisms turn over constantly, generations passing in hours. And yet the culture persists, fed daily by hands that change as surely as the microbes do.

I find this quietly astonishing. A sourdough starter is a kind of agreement between species. The wild yeasts and bacteria get sugar and shelter; we get bread that rises and tastes faintly of tang and time. Neither side fully understands the arrangement, but it holds.

People name their starters. They carry them across oceans in suitcases, dry them into flakes to mail to strangers, and leave instructions for their care in wills. There's something tender about keeping alive a thing that can't thank you, that asks only for regular attention. Skip a week and it sulks, growing a gray layer of liquid called "hooch." Feed it again and it forgives you, bubbling up by morning.

Maybe that's the appeal. So much of modern life is frictionless and instant, but a starter insists on patience. It works on its own schedule, responds to the temperature of your kitchen, and changes subtly depending on the flour you give it and even the air it breathes.

It's a small reminder that some of the best things aren't made. They're tended, passed along, and kept going, one ordinary feeding at a time.
